summary.title: Toxicity of TiO2, SiO2, ZnO, CuO, Au and Ag engineered nanoparticles on hatching and early nauplii of Artemia sp
summary.authors: Ch Lakshmi N Murthy; Mohammed M Idris; Shashi Singh
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the acute toxicity of six engineered nanoparticles (Ag, Au, CuO, ZnO, TiO2, SiO2) and three soluble salts on the hatching and early development of Artemia sp. Given the increasing environmental release of nanomaterials, a simple and efficient test to estimate acute toxicity is required. The authors utilized Artemia cysts and nauplii as model organisms due to their robustness and cost-effectiveness. The study employed two parallel assays: a hatching rate test using hydrated and bleached cysts, and a standard Artemia toxicity test monitoring nauplii viability. Physicochemical characterization via TEM and DLS revealed that nanoparticles exhibited different behaviors in salt water, with some showing flocculation. The results demonstrated a clear order of toxicity: Ag > CuO > ZnO > Au > TiO2 > SiO2. Silver and copper oxide nanoparticles showed the highest toxicity, significantly reducing hatching rates and increasing larval mortality. A strong inverse correlation was found between hatching rates and larval mortality, suggesting that the hatching test can serve as a valid pre-screening tool for nanoparticle hazard assessment. The study also observed oxidative stress markers (ROS) in exposed nauplii, particularly with silver nanoparticles. The findings highlight the utility of Artemia assays for high-throughput screening of nanomaterial toxicity in aquatic environments.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the acute toxicity of six engineered nanoparticles (Ag, Au, CuO, ZnO, TiO2, SiO2) and three soluble salts on the hatching and early development of Artemia sp. Given the increasing environmental release of nanomaterials, a simple and efficient test to estimate acute toxicity is required. The authors utilized Artemia cysts and nauplii as model organisms due to their robustness and cost-effectiveness. The study employed two parallel assays: a hatching rate test using hydrated and bleached cysts, and a standard Artemia toxicity test monitoring nauplii viability. Physicochemical characterization via TEM and DLS revealed that nanoparticles exhibited different behaviors in salt water, with some showing flocculation. The results demonstrated a clear order of toxicity: Ag > CuO > ZnO > Au > TiO2 > SiO2. Silver and copper oxide nanoparticles showed the highest toxicity, significantly reducing hatching rates and increasing larval mortality. A strong inverse correlation was found between hatching rates and larval mortality, suggesting that the hatching test can serve as a valid pre-screening tool for nanoparticle hazard assessment. The study also observed oxidative stress markers (ROS) in exposed nauplii, particularly with silver nanoparticles. The findings highlight the utility of Artemia assays for high-throughput screening of nanomaterial toxicity in aquatic environments.

Research Context
Nanomaterials pose risks to the environment and human health due to expanding applications. There is a lack of information on the impact of nanoscale objects on ecosystems. Aquatic systems are the primary receptacles for released nanomaterials. Artemia sp. are used as a model organism for toxicological assays. Previous studies rarely used hatching of hydrated cysts as a toxicity endpoint.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to estimate the acute toxicity of six nanoparticles on Artemia hatching and nauplii. The hypothesis is that nanoparticles will affect hatching rates and larval viability. The study predicts an order of toxicity based on nanoparticle type. It is hypothesized that hatching rate correlates with larval mortality. The goal is to validate the hatching test as a hazard assessment tool.

Methodological Details
Six nanoparticles (Ag, Au, CuO, ZnO, TiO2, SiO2) and three salts were tested. Nanoparticles were sourced from the NANOVALID project consortium. Artemia cysts (San Francisco Bay strain) were used for cultures. Cysts were hydrated in distilled water and bleached with sodium hypochlorite. Hatching occurred in 25% salt water at 28°C for 24 hours. Nanoparticle concentrations of 100 mg/L and 10 mg/L were used. The standard Artemia toxicity test used concentrations from 100 to 0.01 mg/L. Viability was counted at 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, and 48 hours. Oxidative stress was measured using DCFDA staining. Experiments were repeated six times for statistical validity.

Procedures And Architectures
Nanoparticle suspensions were sonicated at 30W for 10 minutes. TEM was used to characterize nanoparticles on copper grids. DLS was used to measure particle size in water and salt water. Artemia cysts were decapsulated using 20% sodium hypochlorite for 15 minutes. Hatching was monitored under continuous light and aeration. Nauplii were transferred to six-well plates for the toxicity test. Mortality was defined as cessation of swimming or movement. LD50 was calculated using GraphPad software. DCFDA fluorescence was imaged using a Zeiss Axiovert imager. Data was analyzed for correlation using Microsoft Excel.

Key Results
The order of toxicity was estimated as Ag > CuO > ZnO > Au > TiO2 > SiO2. Control hatching rate was 74% ± 5.5 with 97% viability. Silver and CuO reduced hatching rate to about 29% at 100 mg/L. Viability of hatched nauplii in Ag/CuO was 50% at 100 mg/L. Silver nitrate showed 80% mortality in 24 hours. LC50 of silver nanoparticles was around 10.12 mg/L at 24 hours. TiO2 hatching rate was 41.50% at 100 mg/L with 67.8% viability. SiO2 at 10 mg/L showed hatching and viability equivalent to controls. A strong inverse correlation (-0.7853) was found between hatching and mortality. No statistically significant difference was found in mean values (P=0.683).

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The hatching test serves as a valid pre-screening tool for nanoparticle toxicity. Toxicity may be due to ionic forms or gut clogging by nanoparticles. Artemia is a suitable model for assessing nanoparticle behavior in aquatic environments. The assays are easy, short-term, and use mortality as an endpoint. The method allows for high-throughput hazard identification of nanomaterials.

Contradictions And Limitations
Sedimentation and flocculation of nanoparticles may vary between particles. Ionic components may precipitate due to high salinity. The study focuses on acute toxicity, not chronic effects. Morphological abnormalities were not observed despite high toxicity.

Claims
Artemia hatching rate is a sensitive indicator of nanoparticle toxicity. Hatching rate dropped drastically in the presence of nanoparticles. There is a strong correlation between hatching rates and larval mortality. SiO2 at low concentration showed better hatching than control. This assay can be used for high-throughput screening.
Silver and copper oxide nanoparticles are the most toxic to Artemia. Silver and CuO showed the highest effect on hatching. Silver nitrate caused 80% mortality in 24 hours. Viability was better at lower concentrations (10 mg/L). These nanoparticles pose a higher risk to aquatic ecosystems.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Experiments were repeated six times to ensure validity. Validity criterion was low mortality in the control. Correlation tests were performed using online software.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows TEM images of nanoparticles. Figure 2 shows DLS values in water and salt water. Table 1 presents hatching rates and viability data. Figure 3 illustrates hatching rate changes. Table 2 presents larval toxicity and LC50 data. Figure 4 shows mortality over time. Figure 5 shows nanoparticle accumulation in gut. Figure 6 shows correlation between hatching and mortality.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the validation of Artemia hatching as a nanoparticle toxicity assay. 2. The strongest evidence is the strong inverse correlation (-0.7853) between hatching and mortality. 3. The future path is using this assay for high-throughput hazard identification.
